title: A headline earns attention by refusing the wrong reader.
dek: Claude Hopkins treats the headline as the first act of salesmanship, but not as a bid for universal attention. Its job is to make the right prospect recognise a relevant benefit quickly enough to keep reading - and to let everyone else pass by.

marginNote.label: Apprenticeship Note
marginNote.body: Reach is not the same as a hearing. Before polishing a line, name the person who should immediately recognise why it concerns them and the concrete interest that makes it worth their next ten seconds.

canon.heading: Hopkins: The headline is a filter before it is a flourish.
canon.standfirst: Read Chapter 5, "Headlines," from Claude C. Hopkins's Scientific Advertising, through PDF page 14. Hopkins's point is bracingly narrow: a headline should call out the people who can be interested in the offer, reveal the interest at stake, and earn a hearing for the sales argument that follows.
canon.readerIntro: Read once for the distinction between attracting attention and attracting a prospect. Read again for the operating implication: the preferred headline is not the one the writer enjoys; it is the appeal that earns measured response from the intended reader.

blocks.label: 01 / Call the right person, not the whole crowd
paragraphs: Hopkins begins with the asymmetry between a salesperson and an advertisement. A salesperson can force a moment of attention but spends time on people who will never care. An advertisement can be skipped, which makes its first responsibility more precise: identify the people for whom the offer has a live relevance.

His test is simple. If you needed to address one person in a crowd, you would use the signal that lets that person know you mean them. A headline should do the equivalent work: name or imply the relevant need, outcome, situation, or audience before it tries to charm everyone nearby.

blocks.label: 02 / Reveal the interest instead of hiding it
paragraphs: A blind or clever heading may create curiosity, Hopkins concedes, yet curiosity can be badly qualified. It may collect people who cannot use the offer while the people who could use it never realise the advertisement concerns them. His newspaper analogy makes the problem concrete: headlines help readers sort a crowded page by the subjects they already care about.

This is not an argument for flat copy. It is an argument against concealment at the exact moment a busy reader is deciding whether the message belongs in their day. The useful headline converts a real product advantage into an immediately legible reason to continue.

blocks.label: 03 / Let returns overrule the writer's taste
paragraphs: Hopkins gives headlines a commercial burden: an otherwise identical advertisement can produce radically different returns when its entry point changes. That means the writer's preferred appeal is evidence only about the writer. It does not average the desires of the market.

The discipline is to compare relevant appeals and learn which one earns the right kind of response. A product may offer cleanliness, beauty, economy, labour saving, or status; the headline should foreground the live desire for the reader and publication in front of it. Other useful appeals remain available, but they should not be confused with the main door into the message.

closeReading: What is the difference between a headline that wins attention and one that wins a hearing from a prospect?
Why does Hopkins consider a clever but vague headline risky even if it attracts more readers?
Choose an offer you know. Which two distinct desires could truthfully lead its headline, and which audience or context would make each one relevant?
What signal would show that a headline is attracting the wrong people rather than merely underperforming?
Where in your current copy does a reader need to infer the benefit that could instead be revealed at the decision point?

principle.heading: Make the benefit recognisable before you make the line memorable.
principle.body: A headline does not need to explain the entire offer. It needs to make the reader who has the relevant problem, desire, or job recognise that the next sentence may be for them. Start with that selection task, then use testing to discover which truthful entry point earns the best qualified attention.
principle.example: A workflow tool can honestly promise fewer status meetings, faster client approvals, and a reliable audit trail. A homepage headline that says "Work, finally organised" may sound polished but leaves all three audiences guessing. For an agency owner arriving from a search about client feedback, "Get client approvals without another status meeting" makes the benefit and the reader's immediate context visible. The other claims can do useful work below the fold or in tests for different jobs.
principle.practice: Pick one live page, email, or ad. Write the exact reader, the situation that makes them receptive, and the concrete benefit they seek. Draft three headlines that each lead with a different truthful desire. For each, mark the audience it should exclude, the downstream action it should improve, and the evidence you will use to compare it.

signals.heading: Three signals that the opening claim is becoming part of the product decision.

fieldNotes.title: Domino's pays diners to beta test its relaunched app and website
fieldNotes.whatHappened: Domino's is offering qualifying digital-order customers $5 off a later order while inviting feedback on its relaunched website and app, supported by TV, online video, social, and digital activity.
fieldNotes.whyItMatters: The concrete proposition is not simply that a new site exists. It gives an active digital-order customer a reason to try the experience and a specific role in the launch. Hopkins's standard applies: the opening promise works when the relevant reader can quickly see why the message is for them.
fieldNotes.watch: Whether feedback and ordering data reveal a particular customer moment or benefit that becomes more prominent in the next phase of the launch.

fieldNotes.title: Claire's refreshes the piercing service, not just the merchandise
fieldNotes.whatHappened: Claire's is rolling out updated training, store displays, earrings, and related changes as part of a broader upgrade to its in-store piercing service.
fieldNotes.whyItMatters: The commercial object is not merely an earring assortment; it is a confidence-bearing service moment. A headline, offer, or store message that leads with the product category alone can miss the actual reason a first-time customer pauses. The sharper question is which benefit the customer is already looking to recognise.
fieldNotes.watch: Whether Claire's frames and measures the refresh around reassurance, convenience, self-expression, or another specific decision driver rather than a generic service upgrade.

fieldNotes.title: OpenAI's reported speaker price puts the AI-device test in a familiar category
fieldNotes.whatHappened: TechCrunch reports that OpenAI's forthcoming AI device could be a smart-speaker-like product priced between $300 and $400, adding a consumer price anchor to a still indistinct hardware proposition.
fieldNotes.whyItMatters: A new category is especially vulnerable to a vague opening claim. If customers only recognise another speaker, they will compare it on that frame. The launch message needs to surface the distinct recurring job early enough for the intended buyer to understand why the product deserves attention at all.
fieldNotes.watch: Whether the eventual product story leads with a concrete daily use case that differentiates it from conventional voice assistants, rather than only with technology or form factor.

tweets.author: Albinder Dhindsa
tweets.title: A design-first brand enters Blinkit's customer context
tweets.summary: The post marks DailyObjects joining Blinkit's customer-facing range. It is a small distribution reminder for Hopkins's chapter: relevance depends not just on the words in a headline but on whether the offer appears where the intended customer can recognise it as useful.
tweets.text: Back in the day, we (Grofers) were doing B2B deliveries for @daily_objects. More than a decade later, it’s great to see what Pankaj and Saurav have built. A thoughtful, design-first Indian brand with an incredible range of products. And now, we get to help take that range to Blinkit customers.

output.heading: Write the headline your most relevant reader can recognise.
output.body: After reading, produce a three-headline test card for one real offer: the audience and situation, the desired benefit each line reveals, the audience each line excludes, and the behaviour that would tell you which entry point earned the better hearing.
